Narendra Modi Stadium

Narendra Modi Stadium is an international cricket stadium in Motera, Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. With a total capacity of 132,000, it is the world's largest cricket stadium and the largest overall stadium in the world by capacity. It is owned by the Gujarat Cricket Association, and hosts both domestic and international cricket matches. The stadium has hosted several high-profile matches, such as the 2023 Cricket World Cup final and the 2026 Men's T20 World Cup final. The stadium will also be used for the 2030 Commonwealth Games. Situated near the Sabarmati River, the stadium is named after the prime minister of India, Narendra Modi.

It replaced Sardar Patel Gujarat Stadium, which hosted domestic and international cricket in the city until its demolition in 2015, including the 1987, 1996, and 2011 Cricket World Cups. In 2014, it was decided that a new stadium should be built on the same plot. The new stadium, originally named Motera Stadium, was designed by Populous and built by Larsen and Toubro. It took five years to build, at an estimated cost of₹ 800 crore(US$83 million). After completion, the new arena replaced the Melbourne Cricket Ground as the world's largest cricket stadium. The stadium has four dressing rooms, 11 centre pitches, and two practice grounds. The practice grounds can also serve as venues for domestic matches.

On February 24, 2020, the new stadium first opened to the public by hosting the Namaste Trump event, which saw an approximate attendance of 125,000 people. One year later, on February 24, 2021, the stadium was officially inaugurated by Indian president Ram Nath Kovind and renamed "Narendra Modi Stadium" in honour of Modi who had previously served as the Chief Minister of Gujarat (2001–2014) and President of the Gujarat Cricket Association (2009–2014). This ceremony took place just hours before the venue hosted its first-ever international cricket match—a day-night pink-ball Test between India and England.

On 29 September 2022, the opening ceremony of the 2022 National Games of India was held in the stadium.

## Planning and construction

### Conception

The idea to build a new stadium was proposed by Narendra Modi himself who was the president of the Gujarat Cricket Association and the Chief Minister of Gujarat at the same time. Shortly before Modi moved to Delhi after becoming the prime minister of India, there were discussions about adding minor upgrades to the stadium and further developing areas of the structure at the pavilion end. Modi asked officials to build a new, larger stadium instead of pursuing minor renovation work.

US president Donald Trump and Indian prime minister Narendra Modi at the Narendra Modi Stadium, 24 February 2020.

In October 2015, the stadium was demolished for reconstruction, though some media referred to it as a renovation. The total cost of reconstruction was estimated to be₹ 700 crores(₹7 billion (US$73 million)). However, the final cost was reported at ₹800 crore (US$83 million). The redevelopment, originally planned to be completed in 2019, finished in February 2020.

### Bids

After starting demolition work at the end of 2015, the GCA issued a request for tender on 1 January 2016 in The Times of India and The Indian Express. Nine bidders showed interest and purchased the tender documents, out of which three submitted technical and financial bids on time; they were the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, Nagarjuna Construction Company, and Larsen & Toubro(L&T). A Tender Commercial Committee (TCC) of nine experts was formed to evaluate tenders. Additionally, STUP Consultants, a civil engineering consultancy firm based in Mumbai, was appointed as the project management consultant to evaluate proposals and technical details of each bid working with the TCC.

Each of the three bidders presented their designs, models, and technical details of their concepts and designs. Due to the sheer size and complexity of the project, the bidders were evaluated on many parameters. These included efficiency, resources, project length, and ease of implementation, among others. The bidders were ranked and weighted based on the parameters.

In the end, Larsen & Turbo was selected as the stadium's principal contractor.

### Building work

L&T took over the construction work of the stadium in December 2016. On 16 January 2017, the Gujarat Cricket Association oversaw the project, which formally began on the same day. The stadium was planned to be finished in 2 years, and the reconstruction project was estimated to cost around ₹700 crore ($93 million). Final completion of the stadium was finished in February 2020, and it hosted an England- India day-night test match in 2021.

Mumbai-based commercial kitchen consultant "Span Asia" was hired to collaborate with Populous and L&T on food and beverage-related areas such as concession counters, main stadium kitchens, player kitchens, VIP/VVIP boxes, corporate boxes, press & media boxes, pantries, the GCA Club, and related areas.

## Service

In 2020, the event " Namaste Trump" was organized at the stadium for the visit of US president Donald J. Trump. 125,000 attendees were recorded. Before it became clear that the complex would continue to use the name "Sardar Patel Sports Enclave" and that only the stadium would receive a new name, Congress first criticized the decision.

Prime Minister Modi inaugurated the 2022 National Games of India in the arena.

The stadium later became the home ground of IPL team Gujarat Titans and hosted the 2022, 2023, and 2025 IPL Finals.

The stadium also hosted five matches of the 2023 Cricket World Cup, including the opening and final games, as well as high-profile matches pitting India against Pakistan and Australia against England.

British rock band Coldplay played two shows at the stadium on 25 and 26 January 2025, as part of their Music of the Spheres World Tour.

## Design and facilities

The Stadium during the 2023 Cricket World Cup final between India and Australia

The stadium is built on 63 acres of land and has four entry points, with a metro line at one of the entry points. It has 76 corporate boxes that can hold 25 persons each, a 55-room clubhouse, an Olympic size swimming pool, and four dressing rooms. A food court and hospitality area are available in each spectator stand. The stadium also includes an indoor cricket academy and practice pitches, with dormitories for 40 athletes.

The stands generally follow a two-tier structure; however, there is a three-tier main pavilion. The two-tier structure is supported from beneath by numerous Y-shaped columns, which eliminate the need for pillars and thus give spectators an unobstructed view of the entire field from all parts of the stadium. An LED light system lines the stadium roof's inside edge. This eliminates the need for floodlights and helps reduce shadows on the pitch. The LED lights are installed on an antibacterial, fireproof canopy with PTFE membrane that covers 30 metres (98 ft) out of 55 metres (180 ft) width of the seating area. The roof was installed by Walter P. Moore, and was specifically designed to be lightweight and separate from the seating bowls in order to improve earthquake resistance.

The ground has 11 center pitches. The playing field has sensors to detect the need for water for the grass, which can automatically activate 67 fully automated underground pop-up sprinklers. The ground surface is made of Bermuda grass. The stadium has an extensive drainage system.

The stadium premises have many facilities, including an indoor cricket practice area, badminton, tennis, and squash courts, a table tennis area, a 3D projector theatre, three practice grounds, and 50 rooms. The parking lot can accommodate 3,000 cars and 10,000 two-wheelers. A ramp leading to the stadium is designed to facilitate the movement of around 60,000 people simultaneously. The arena has been designed in such a way that the upper stands can remain empty (such as during smaller events) while maintaining a sufficient crowd atmosphere. However, a game between Royal Challengers Bangalore and Rajasthan Royals in the IPL 2024 saw a near houseful crowd of over 1 lakh.

There was a plan that the stadium would be connected to the nearest metro station by a skywalk bridge in order to decrease road congestion. Construction was planned to be completed after September 2020. As of November 2023, the skywalk is yet to be constructed.

## Political events

### Namaste Trump

The stadium during the Namaste Trump event, as US president Donald Trump gives a speech

In 2020, the stadium was the venue of the "Namaste Trump" event, which was organized for the maiden visit of US president Donald Trump to India by Indian prime minister Narendra Modi. The event mirrored the " Howdy Modi" event held in Houston, Texas, US.

### 75 years of Friendship through Cricket

On 9 March 2023, Narendra Modi Stadium hosted the 75 Years of Friendship through Cricket Event, which was attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and visiting Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese. The event was held in conjunction with the fourth Test match of the Border-Gavaskar Trophy between India and Australia.

The event began with the two prime ministers singing the national anthems of their respective countries and shaking hands with the players of both teams. They then visited a gallery showcasing glimpses of 75 years of cricket friendship between the two countries. After the gallery visit, the two prime ministers took a lap of honor around the stadium in a specially designed golf cart. They were greeted by loud cheers from the crowd, who waved Indian and Australian flags. The event concluded with the two prime ministers tossing the coin to start the Test match.

The 75 Years of Friendship through Cricket Event was a celebration of the strong ties between India and Australia, which have been forged over many years through the shared love of cricket. The event was also an opportunity to promote sports diplomacy and to encourage people from both countries to come together and celebrate their friendship.

## Domestic cricket

The stadium is the home ground of the Gujarat cricket team, the Gujarat women's cricket team, and the IPL franchise Gujarat Titans. Other than the main ground inside the stadium, it also has two grounds known as "Narendra Modi Stadium A Ground" and "Narendra Modi Stadium B Ground", which are located near the stadium on the eastern side. They host domestic cricket matches for tournaments such as the Ranji Trophy. The stadium hosted the 2022 and 2023 IPL finals. In 2022, the home team Gujarat Titans prevailed; in 2023, the Chennai Super Kings won their fifth title. The 2022 final for the Vijay Hazare Trophy was held inside the arena. Maharashtra scored 248/9 in first innings; Saurashtra chased down it in 46.3 overs. Maharashtra's Ruturaj Gaikwad and Saurashtra's Sheldon Jackson scored hundreds.

## Notable achievements

- On 24 February 2021, the arena hosted its first Day/night Test, with India facing off against England.
- In 2022, the arena hosted the IPL final between the Gujarat Titans and the Rajasthan Royals. The Titans won the IPL in their inaugural season. This event was attended by 104,859 people, the highest attendance in the history of the stadium and cricket in general.
- In the 2023 IPL final between the Gujarat Titans and Chennai Super Kings(CSK), MS Dhoni(playing in his 250th match) captained CSK to their fifth IPL victory, tying the Mumbai Indians for the record of most IPL trophies.
- In the 2026 Men's T20 World Cup, India defeated New Zealand in the final held here, thus becoming the only team to win back-to-back T20 World Cups (2024 and 2026), and a record three titles in the T20 World Cup.
- In the 2025 and 2026 IPL finals, Royal Challengers Bengaluru defeated Punjab Kings and Gujarat Titans respectively to win their first two titles. RCB thus retained the title successfully.

## List criteria notes

- The capacity figures are standard, permanent total capacity, including both seating and any permanent standing areas, but excluding any temporary accommodation.
- Incidental record attendance is not considered relevant. Only regular capacity counts; for attendance records, see List of sporting venues with a highest attendance of 100,000 or more.
- Only stadiums with a capacity of 40,000 or more are included in this list.
- Stadiums that are defunct or closed, or those that no longer serve as competitive sports venues (such as Great Strahov Stadium, which was the largest in the world and held around 250,000 spectators), are not included. They are listed under List of closed stadiums by capacity.
- An asterisk (*) indicates that the team plays only some (few) of its home matches at the venue, and may have another (primary) home ground.
- For purposes of this list, race tracks (such as the Indianapolis Motor Speedway and the Tokyo Racecourse) are not stadiums, and are not included here. For a list of all sports venues by capacity, see List of sports venues by capacity.
- Capacities are taken whenever possible from the figure stated on the official website of a stadium, its tenants, or sports event it has hosted.

# The Largest Stadium in the World and 9 Massive Contenders

By: Mitch Ryan| Aug 22, 2024

While you may think of the Super Bowl, FIFA World Cup or Olympics when imagining the largest stadiums in the world, the No. 1 biggest is considered the capital of cricket. Dmytro Aksonov / Getty Images

Professional and college athletics is a massive market that brings in hundreds of billions of dollars each year, but a large part of those proceeds come from the venue. People come from all around to gather in a stadium, arena or similar venue to cheer on their team and bask in the energy of live sports (and sometimes even massive concerts).

The bigger the buzz, the bigger the stadium you need to hold these massive audiences, but which is the largest stadium in the world?

The world's largest stadiums are the few venues with sufficient seating capacity for sold-out superstar concerts, the FIFA World Cup and the Olympics.

## 1. The World's Largest Cricket Stadium: Narendra Modi Stadium, India (Capacity: 132,000)

It might interest casual fans to learn that cricket is the sport that birthed the world's largest stadium, and the capital of cricket is Narendra Modi Stadium in India. Built on the ruins of Sardar Patel Stadium in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, this mammoth structure can hold roughly 132,000 screaming fans.

## 2. Rungrado 1st Of May Stadium, North Korea (Capacity: 114,000)

Although the Melbourne Cricket Ground in Victoria, Australia, is often regarded as the second-biggest stadium for cricket, the silver medal for our list goes to this multipurpose stadium in Pyongyang, North Korea.

Although some events have allowed foreign spectators, it is obviously more difficult for Americans to make it to a game at Rungrado than one at your local average arena.

## 3. Michigan Stadium, U.S. (Capacity: 107,601)

American football reigns supreme in the States, and there's no place like "The Big House" at Michigan Stadium to watch a game. Smack-dab in the heart of Ann Arbor, Michigan Stadium has been the home of the Wolverines since 1927. It's also, of course, the largest college football stadium in the U.S.

## 4. Beaver Stadium, U.S. (Capacity: 106,572)

The second-largest college football stadium and fourth-largest stadium in the world is the home of the Penn State Nittany Lions: Beaver Stadium. Located in University Park, Beaver Stadium can hold just over 106,000 fans.

## 5. Ohio Stadium, U.S. (Capacity: 102,780)

Ohio Stadium, home of the Ohio State Buckeyes, is steeped in college football heritage. Since its opening in 1922, over 40 million fans have swarmed to Columbus, Ohio, to cheer on their BIG 10 dynasty.

## 6. Kyle Field, U.S. (Capacity: 102,733)

Head to College Station, Texas, to catch the Texas A&M Aggies as they take on the competition at their home stadium at Kyle Field. Kyle Field has come a long way from its humble beginnings of a $500 covered grandstand in 1904 to one of the largest stadiums in the world.

## 7. Tiger Stadium, U.S. (Capacity: 102,321)

Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, can hold a sold-out crowd of over 102,000 purple-and-yellow-clad college football fans every game day.

## 8. Neyland Stadium, U.S. (Capacity: 101,915)

University of Tennessee's Big Orange Faithful have flocked to Neyland Stadium for over a century. It is the sixth-largest stadium in the country and eighth-largest in the world.

## 9. Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium, U.S. (Capacity: 100,119)

Hook Em' Longhorns live at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin. Baseball may be huge in the state, but there is no feeling like catching a football game under the big lights in the Lone Star State.

## 10. Bryant-Denny Stadium, U.S. (Capacity: 100,077)

Any opposing football team that has ever stepped foot in Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, knows that they may be facing an unstoppable rollin' Tide on any given night. Witnessing a game here is a crowning jewel for any fan of sporting events.

Now That's Ancient

Stadium was once a unit of measure in ancient Greece, equal to 1/8 mile or roughly 200 meters. The Colosseum of Rome, Italy, is one of the most famous stadiums in history, but it was one of many in a long tradition of sports and celebrations. Other notable stadiums include those at Pompeii, Delphi and Athens.

10 Biggest Stadiums in the World (2026) - City Viking

Source: legio09 on Flickr| CC BY-SA 2.0

Ask what the biggest stadium in the world is and the answer surprises almost everyone. It is not a soccer cathedral in Europe or an NFL palace in the United States, but a cricket ground in western India that swallows a small city's worth of spectators in a single afternoon. Ranked strictly by official seating capacity, the ten largest stadiums on Earth are a curious mix: one Indian cricket giant, one enigmatic North Korean showpiece, and a run of American college-football coliseums that most of the world has never heard of.

That last fact is the real story of this list. Once you clear the top two, the entire hundred-thousand-seat tier belongs to United States college football, where Saturday crowds regularly outdraw the biggest professional leagues on the planet. This is a countdown of operational venues you could, in theory, buy a ticket to today, ordered from largest to smallest by the seats they hold. The gaps at the top are enormous and the finish is a photo, with four stadiums separated by barely two thousand seats.

## The Ranking at a Glance

1Narendra Modi Stadium132,000 seats

India 2Rungrado 1st of May Stadium113,281 seats

North Korea 3Michigan Stadium107,601 seats

United States 4Beaver Stadium106,572 seats

United States 5Ohio Stadium102,780 seats

United States 8Neyland Stadium101,915 seats

United States 9Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium100,119 seats

United States 10Bryant–Denny Stadium100,077 seats

## Fun Facts About the World's Biggest Stadiums

- The largest stadium on Earth is a cricket ground, not a soccer or football venue — India's Narendra Modi Stadium seats 132,000.
- Eight of the ten biggest stadiums in the world are American college-football venues, most in the U.S. South and Midwest.
- Four of the top ten are separated by fewer than 3,000 seats, all clustered just above the 100,000-seat mark.
- North Korea's Rungrado 1st of May Stadium — the world's second-largest — has a roof made of 16 arches shaped like a magnolia blossom.
- Ohio Stadium is one of the very few stadiums listed on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places.

## Map of Biggest Stadiums in the World

Biggest Stadiums in the World

## 1. Narendra Modi StadiumIndia

132,000 seats

Source: A Cricket Premi on Wikimedia| CC BY-SA 4.0

With a seating capacity of 132,000, the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad is the largest stadium in the world and the largest cricket ground ever built, dwarfing the runner-up by nearly twenty thousand seats. Rebuilt from the ground up and reopened in 2020 on the site of the old Motera stadium, its clean, bowl-like design gives every one of those seats an unobstructed view of the pitch, an engineering feat at this scale.

The stadium anchors a vast sports complex beside the Sabarmati River and has quickly become the beating heart of Indian cricket, hosting marquee internationals including a Cricket World Cup final. For a first-time visitor, the sheer scale is the spectacle: a sea of orange seats sweeping around the field in an unbroken ring, with room for more people than live in many world capitals.

## 2. Rungrado 1st of May StadiumNorth Korea

113,281 seats

Source: Christophe95 on Wikimedia| CC BY-SA 4.0

The Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in Pyongyang holds 113,281 spectators, making it the second-largest stadium on Earth and the biggest outside of India. Opened in 1989 on an island in the Taedong River, its unmistakable roof is formed from sixteen arches arranged in a ring, a silhouette often likened to a magnolia blossom floating above the water.

More than a sports arena, it is a stage for North Korea's famous mass games, choreographed spectacles involving tens of thousands of performers in perfect unison. The scalloped roof, the enormous playing field, and the tiered stands make it one of the most visually distinctive stadiums anywhere, a monument built as much for pageantry as for football and athletics.

## 3. Michigan StadiumUnited States

107,601 seats

Source: Allen Boguslavsky on Pexels(illustrative image)

Known to everyone in college football simply as The Big House, Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor seats 107,601, making it the largest stadium in the United States and the Western Hemisphere. Home to the University of Michigan Wolverines, it packs a crowd larger than the entire population of Ann Arbor into a single afternoon roughly half a dozen times each autumn.

What startles first-time visitors is how deceptive it looks from outside: much of the bowl is sunk below ground level, so the stadium reveals its true, staggering depth only once you walk in and look down. On a home Saturday the noise and the maize-and-blue wall of humanity make it one of the great sensory experiences in American sport.

## 4. Beaver StadiumUnited States

106,572 seats

Source: Caitlinator on Flickr| CC BY 2.0

Beaver Stadium at Penn State holds 106,572 fans, ranking it the fourth-largest stadium in the world and a perennial rival to Michigan for the title of biggest in the United States. Set among the rolling hills of University Park, it is the home of the Nittany Lions and the crucible for one of college football's most feared traditions, the White Out, when the entire crowd dresses in white and the stands turn into a single blinding mass.

The stadium has grown by repeated expansion since 1960 and continues to evolve through an ongoing renovation that could push its capacity even higher in the years ahead. Visitors consistently rank a night game here among the loudest, most intimidating atmospheres anywhere in the sport, the sound trapped and amplified by the stadium's steep, towering decks.

## 5. Ohio StadiumUnited States

102,780 seats

Source: dankeck on Flickr| CC0 1.0

Ohio Stadium in Columbus seats 102,780, making it the fifth-largest stadium in the world and the home of the Ohio State Buckeyes since it opened in 1922. Nicknamed The Horseshoe for its distinctive U-shaped bowl, its double-decked stands and closed end have been expanded over a century into one of the most recognizable structures in American sport.

Unlike the purely functional coliseums that surround it on this list, Ohio Stadium is an architectural landmark in its own right, a rare stadium listed on the National Register of Historic Places. On game day its horseshoe shape channels the roar of more than a hundred thousand scarlet-clad fans down onto the field, and the marching band's ramp entrance is a spectacle in itself.

## 6. Kyle FieldUnited States

102,733 seats

Source: Janreagan at English Wikipedia on Wikimedia| CC BY-SA 4.0

Kyle Field, the home of Texas A&M in College Station, holds 102,733 spectators, making it the sixth-largest stadium in the world and the biggest in the Southeastern Conference. A sweeping redevelopment turned it into a fully enclosed, steep-sided bowl designed to trap and hurl sound back onto the field, and it delivers: the venue is famous as one of the loudest in college football.

Aggie tradition sets Kyle Field apart from any other stadium on Earth. The student body stands for the entire game, a custom called the Twelfth Man that treats the crowd itself as an extra player, and the whole stadium sways together during yell practice. It is less a place to watch a game than to take part in one.

## 7. Tiger StadiumUnited States

102,321 seats

Source: VasenkaPhotography on Flickr| CC BY 2.0

Tiger Stadium at LSU in Baton Rouge seats 102,321, ranking it the seventh-largest stadium in the world and one of the most storied venues in American sport. Its nickname, Death Valley, is a warning to visiting teams, and its reputation for deafening night games under the Louisiana sky is the stuff of college-football legend.

The atmosphere here is so intense that a roaring crowd once registered on a seismograph as a small earthquake, an event fans still recount with pride. Wrapped tightly around the field with towering upper decks, Tiger Stadium concentrates the energy of more than a hundred thousand people into a wall of sound that few opponents ever get used to.

## 8. Neyland StadiumUnited States

101,915 seats

Source: Steve DiMatteo on Pexels(illustrative image)

Neyland Stadium in Knoxville holds 101,915 fans, making it the eighth-largest stadium in the world and the home of the Tennessee Volunteers. Perched on the banks of the Tennessee River, it enjoys one of the most scenic settings of any major stadium, and on game day the water fills with the Vol Navy, a flotilla of boats that ferry fans to the game by river.

The sea of orange that floods the stands is one of college football's signature sights, and the pregame ritual of running through the T formed by the marching band is a tradition generations of fans have grown up with. Expanded steadily across the decades, Neyland remains among the largest and most atmospheric arenas in the American South.

## 9. Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial StadiumUnited States

100,119 seats

Source: Randall Chancellor on Wikimedia| CC BY-SA 2.0

The Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin seats 100,119, making it the ninth-largest stadium in the world and the home of the Texas Longhorns. Named for the university's legendary coach, it sits just east of downtown Austin and forms the emotional center of one of the most passionate fan bases in the sport.

Game days here paint the Texas capital in burnt orange, and the crowd's Hook 'em Horns hand sign becomes a stadium-wide gesture repeated a hundred thousand times over. Repeated expansions have lifted it past the six-figure mark, and its position in a fast-growing city keeps it firmly among the giants of college football.

## 10. Bryant–Denny StadiumUnited States

100,077 seats

Source: Joel יוֹאֵל on Wikimedia| CC BY-SA 2.0

Rounding out the top ten, Bryant–Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa holds 100,077 spectators, making it the tenth-largest stadium in the world and the home of the Alabama Crimson Tide. Named jointly for onetime university president George Denny and the celebrated coach Paul Bear Bryant, it is the fortress of one of the most successful programs in college-football history.

The stadium has been enlarged repeatedly to keep pace with the Crimson Tide's dynasty, and its crowd of more than a hundred thousand generates an atmosphere every bit as formidable as the team's record. Walking the concourses, visitors pass statues of championship-winning coaches, a reminder that at Bryant–Denny the history is as heavy as the crowds are large.

## FAQ: The World's Biggest Stadiums

### What is the biggest stadium in the world?

The biggest stadium in the world is the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad, India, with a seating capacity of 132,000. It is also the largest cricket stadium ever built, seating nearly 20,000 more spectators than the second-place Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in North Korea.

### Why are so many of the biggest stadiums American college-football venues?

Eight of the ten largest stadiums are U.S. college-football grounds because American universities draw enormous Saturday crowds, often larger than professional leagues. Schools like Michigan, Penn State and Ohio State have expanded their stadiums for a century to hold well over 100,000 fans each.

### What is the biggest stadium in the United States?

Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor, known as The Big House, is the biggest stadium in the United States and the entire Western Hemisphere, seating 107,601. It is the home of the University of Michigan Wolverines and ranks third-largest in the world overall.

### Are these stadiums ranked by capacity or by physical size?

This countdown ranks stadiums strictly by official seating capacity — the number of spectators they hold — not by land area or footprint. Every venue on the list is currently operational, so in principle you could attend an event at any of them today.

### Is the biggest stadium in the world a soccer stadium?

No. Surprisingly, none of the top three are primarily soccer venues. The largest is a cricket ground, the second is a multi-purpose athletics and football stadium, and the rest of the top ten are American college-football stadiums. Europe's largest soccer stadiums fall just outside this list.

Every two years, we watch Olympic athletes compete at some of the world’s largest sporting venues. This year, more than 10,000 athletes competed in the 35 venues designated for the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, including the Stade de France, the country’s largest stadium.

Created for the 1998 Football World Cup, the Stade de France has hosted World Athletics Championships, Rugby World Cups and a Euro Football Championship. It can seat more than 80,000 fans, according to the Paris Tourist Office.

But while the Stade de France’s seating capacity may sound gargantuan, it doesn’t even crack the top 10 list.

## What is the biggest stadium?

Located in Pyongyang, North Korea, the Rungrado 1st of May Stadium is the largest stadium in the world. It has 150,000 seats and a total floor area of over 2.2 million square feet. It stands eight stories high.

Rungrado 1st of May Stadium – also known as the May Day stadium – was built with its overpowering size in mind. North Korea constructed the stadium in 1989 during the Cold War, just a year after South Korea hosted the Summer Olympics. Tensions between the North and the South caused the two nations to look for any opportunity to one-up each other. This resulted in North Korea creating an Olympics-style competition of its own, expanding a major airport and constructing new streets, a skyscraper and the May Day stadium, which cost $200 million to build, The New York Times reported.

However, it’s not the only stadium that can fit over 100,000 people. Here are the top 10 largest stadiums in the world and their capacities, according to the International Olympic Committee and official seating records:

1. Rungrado 1st of May Stadium (Pyongyang, North Korea): 150,000
2. Narendra Modi Stadium (Ahmedabad, India): 132,000
3. Michigan Stadium (Michigan, U.S.): 107,601

## What is the largest stadium in the U.S.?

The largest stadium in the U.S. is Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor, Michigan. It’s dubbed “The Big House” for a reason – the University of Michigan sports arena has a seating capacity of 107,601, making it the largest stadium in college football, in the U.S. and even in the entire western hemisphere. It was ranked No. 3 this year in an ESPN ranking of the best stadiums in college football, coming in behind LSU’s Tiger Stadium and UCLA’s Rose Bowl.

Though not technically stadiums, there are many U.S. motor speedways with seating capacities that rival the largest stadiums in the country. For example, the Bristol Motor Speedway in Tennessee, which has a“stadium-like structure,” has a spectator capacity of 162,000, according to NASCAR. The Texas Motor Speedway has a seating capacity of about 150,000 but has seen crowds of over 200,000, Texas Monthly reports.

# What is the biggest stadium in the world? See which have the highest capacity.

Clare Mulroy

USA TODAY

July 28, 2024Updated Nov. 19, 2024, 5:39 p.m. ET

Share to Twitter Share by email

Every two years, we watch Olympic athletes compete at some of the world’s largest sporting venues. This year, more than 10,000 athletes competed in the 35 venues designated for the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, including the Stade de France, the country’s largest stadium.

Created for the 1998 Football World Cup, the Stade de France has hosted World Athletics Championships, Rugby World Cups and a Euro Football Championship. It can seat more than 80,000 fans, according to the Paris Tourist Office.

But while the Stade de France’s seating capacity may sound gargantuan, it doesn’t even crack the top 10 list.

## What is the biggest stadium?

Located in Pyongyang, North Korea, the Rungrado 1st of May Stadium is the largest stadium in the world. It has 150,000 seats and a total floor area of over 2.2 million square feet. It stands eight stories high.

Rungrado 1st of May Stadium – also known as the May Day stadium – was built with its overpowering size in mind. North Korea constructed the stadium in 1989 during the Cold War, just a year after South Korea hosted the Summer Olympics. Tensions between the North and the South caused the two nations to look for any opportunity to one-up each other. This resulted in North Korea creating an Olympics-style competition of its own, expanding a major airport and constructing new streets, a skyscraper and the May Day stadium, which cost $200 million to build, The New York Times reported.

However, it’s not the only stadium that can fit over 100,000 people. Here are the top 10 largest stadiums in the world and their capacities, according to the International Olympic Committee and official seating records:

1. Rungrado 1st of May Stadium (Pyongyang, North Korea): 150,000
2. Narendra Modi Stadium (Ahmedabad, India): 132,000
3. Michigan Stadium (Michigan, U.S.): 107,601
4. Beaver Stadium (Pennsylvania, U.S.): 106,572
5. Ohio Stadium (Ohio, U.S.): 102,780
6. Kyle Field (Texas, U.S.): 102,733
7. Tiger Stadium (Louisiana, U.S.): 102,321
8. Neyland Stadium (Tennessee, U.S.): 101,915
9. Bryant-Denny Stadium (Alabama, U.S.): 101,821
10. Darrel K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium (Texas, U.S.): 100,119

## What is the largest stadium in the U.S.?

The largest stadium in the U.S. is Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor, Michigan. It’s dubbed “The Big House” for a reason – the University of Michigan sports arena has a seating capacity of 107,601, making it the largest stadium in college football, in the U.S. and even in the entire western hemisphere. It was ranked No. 3 this year in an ESPN ranking of the best stadiums in college football, coming in behind LSU’s Tiger Stadium and UCLA’s Rose Bowl.

Here are the top 10 largest college football stadiums in the U.S., according to the NCAA:

1. Michigan Stadium (Ann Arbor, Michigan): 107,601
2. Beaver Stadium (University Park, Pennsylvania): 106,572
3. Ohio Stadium (Columbus, Ohio): 102,780
4. Kyle Field (College Station, Texas): 102,733
5. Tiger Stadium (Baton Rouge, Louisiana): 102,321

8. Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium (Austin, Texas): 100,119
9. Sanford Stadium (Athens, Georgia): 92,746
10. Rose Bowl (Pasadena, California): 91,136

Though not technically stadiums, there are many U.S. motor speedways with seating capacities that rival the largest stadiums in the country. For example, the Bristol Motor Speedway in Tennessee, which has a“stadium-like structure,” has a spectator capacity of 162,000, according to NASCAR. The Texas Motor Speedway has a seating capacity of about 150,000 but has seen crowds of over 200,000, Texas Monthly reports.

# Eight record-breaking stadiums from biggest to most expensive

Published: 2026-07-30T10:00:37+00:00
Source: dezeen.com (dezeen.com)
Language: en

## Story

Stadiums are often vying to be record-breaking structures. To conclude our Future Stadium series, we look at those that top the lists, from the biggest and tallest to the most expensive.

Biggest by capacity and size: Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, Pyongyang, North Korea

Claiming the title for largest in both size and capacity is North Korea's Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, which is distinguished by its unique roof composed of 16 sweeping, concrete arches.

Encompassing 207,000 square metres, the multi-purpose stadium boasts a capacity of 150,000 across eight levels and contains a 22,500-square-metre main arena alongside tracks, training halls and indoor pools.

Completed in 2020 at a cost of $5.5 billion, the SoFi Stadium in the Inglewood area of Los Angeles is the most expensive stadium ever built.

Its expansive structure, which holds 70,000 seats beneath a large curved roof, was designed by architecture studio HKS for development company Kroenke Sports & Entertainment to embody "the spirit of southern California".

A 165-metre-tall office tower beside the Montreal Olympic Stadium in Canada renders the concrete sports venue the tallest stadium in the world.

Originally realised by French architect Roger Taillibert for Montreal's 1976 summer Olympics, the stadium and its adjoining tower remain in use, with its retractable roof and interiors currently being revamped.

Engineering firm Arup led the design for the world's largest free-spanning dome, which shelters the multipurpose Singapore National Stadium.

Spanning 310 metres, the dome crowns the 55,000-seat multipurpose venue and features a retractable roof complete with an integrated lighting system.

Completed in 2022, The Climate Pledge Arena became the first arena in the world to achieve Zero Carbon certification by the International Living Future Institute (ILFI).

Its structure was originally built for the 1962 World's Fair before being revamped by architecture studio Populous in line with sustainability initiatives set out by tech giant Amazon's Climate Pledge.

Designed by British studio Foster + Partners, London's Wembley Stadium is the largest stadium in the UK and features the longest single span roof support structure in the world.

The distinctive Wembley Arch has a steel lattice structure that stretches 315 metres over the 90,000-seat stadium, eliminating the need for any pillars to support the weight of its retractable roof.

Somewhat contentiously holding the spot as the longest-occupied stadium is the Deepdale stadium in England, which is home to Preston North End football team.

Built in 1875, the stadium has been in continuous use since 1878, with gradual additions over the years expanding its capacity to 23,000.

Perched 4,338 metres above sea level in the city of Cerro de Pasco, the Estadio Daniel Alcides Carrión is recognised by global football association FIFA as the highest stadium in the world.

The open-air venue holds up to 12,000 people and serves as the home ground for Peruvian football teams Unión Minas and Ecosem Pasco.

The largest stadiums in the world are a study in contrasts. The biggest holds 132,000 people; the second-biggest holds 113,000. Yet on this ranking the second-largest finishes dead last, and the reason is the whole point of measuring more than one thing. A stadium's capacity tells you how many people it could hold. It does not tell you whether anyone actually shows up.

Seven of these eight are routinely packed to the rafters. One is a near-empty monument. We rank by size first, because the list is about the biggest stadiums on Earth, but we let fill rate, prestige, and access decide the order beneath the leader and expose the one giant that does not belong near the top. For more on where crowds really gather, see our most-visited countries and best live music cities rankings.

## How We Rank the Largest Stadiums in the World

## Methodology

This ranking uses the WorldRankd Composite Index (WURSA). Capacity is the dominant pillar, so the biggest stadiums rise to the top, but four other pillars decide the order beneath it, and that gap between size and substance is what this ranking measures.

Scoring Pillars

Capacity50%

official permanent seating capacity, benchmarked against a major stadium (about 50,000 seats = 5.0) and a world-class ceiling of 150,000 seats (10.0)

Fill Rate18%

how consistently the stadium actually fills, not just its theoretical maximum (a WorldRankd assessment from attendance patterns and tenant schedules)

Prestige12%

the significance of the events it hosts and its standing in world sport

Atmosphere12%

the venue's reputation as a place, its noise, its traditions, and how intimidating or iconic the matchday feels

Access8%

location, transport, and the matchday experience

Capacity figures are official (Wikipedia/ISBC permanent capacities). Fill rate, prestige, atmosphere, and access are WorldRankd editorial assessments anchored to a global standard, not against the other stadiums here.

Compiled by the WorldRankd Data Team.

From sold-out college cathedrals to a cricket colossus and one famously empty giant, here are the eight largest stadiums in the world.

Honest Tradeoff

Rungrado is the second-largest stadium in the world by capacity, but with no regular ticketed tenant it is almost always near-empty, so it ranks last once fill rate and prestige are counted.

This is the upset the whole ranking is built around. The Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in Pyongyang is the second-largest stadium on the planet, and it finishes dead last here, a drop of six places from where its size alone would put it. It was built between 1986 and 1989 on an islet in the Taedong River, and for years its capacity was reported as 150,000 before being revised down to its current figure. Its roof is formed of 16 arches arranged in a ring, meant to resemble a magnolia blossom.

The reason it collapses down the ranking is that it has no regular ticketed tenant. Its defining event is the Mass Games, a choreographed state spectacle that has involved as many as 100,000 performers at once, staged for the government rather than for paying weekend crowds. Set that against Michigan Stadium, which is 5,680 seats smaller at 107,601 yet draws six-figure crowds a dozen Saturdays every autumn. The North Korea national football team nominally plays here, but the venue sits empty far more often than it fills. That is why its fill-rate and atmosphere pillars are the two lowest marks anywhere on this list, and why a stadium 11,366 seats larger than Ohio Stadium ranks seven places below it. Rungrado is a monument to raw scale, stripped of the crowds that give scale its meaning.

Neyland reliably fills with over 100,000 fans, but it sits at the bottom of the college giants on raw capacity and has a slightly narrower national profile than the names above it.

Neyland Stadium in Knoxville opened on September 24, 1921, which makes it 104 years old and the second-oldest venue on this list. It has been through more than a dozen expansions since, growing from a modest grandstand into a six-figure cathedral, and its record crowd of 109,061 packed in to watch the Tennessee Volunteers. Its most famous quirk is the Vol Navy, a flotilla of nearly 200 boats that sails down the Tennessee River and docks outside to tailgate before kickoff, a tradition running since 1962.

On the dominant capacity pillar Neyland is the smallest of the seven American college stadiums here at 101,915, which is what settles it at seventh. But the gap is razor-thin: just 406 seats separate it from Tiger Stadium three places above it, and only 5,686 from Beaver Stadium. On fill rate it scores 9.0, comfortably ahead of the two largest venues on the entire list, both of which fill far less reliably than a Tennessee home Saturday. What keeps Neyland at seventh rather than higher is a slightly narrower national profile than the blueblood programs above it, whose stadiums carry more championship history. It is the clearest proof that near the top of this ranking, a few hundred seats and a sliver of prestige are all that separate one giant from the next.

Kyle Field's 12th Man tradition makes it one of the loudest venues in sport, but its national prestige sits a notch below the bluebloods of Michigan, Ohio State, and LSU.

Kyle Field in College Station first opened in 1905, making it the oldest venue on this list at 121 years, though almost nothing of the original survives: it has been rebuilt and expanded at least eight times, most dramatically in a 2014 to 2015 redevelopment that pushed capacity past 102,000. Its record crowd of 110,633 turned up on October 11, 2014. The stadium is home to the 12th Man, the Texas A&M tradition in which the entire student section stands for the full 60 minutes, symbolically ready to step onto the field.

That standing, roaring student wall makes Kyle Field one of the loudest venues in sport, which is why its atmosphere pillar scores 9.5, tied for the highest here. It fills reliably too, so on the raw numbers it belongs squarely among the giants. What holds it at sixth is prestige: at 102,733 seats it sits just 447 above Tiger Stadium and 47 below Ohio Stadium, an almost invisible gap, and the tiebreaker is national title history. The blueblood programs ranked above it have won more, and more recently, on the biggest stages. Kyle Field wins the noise contest and loses the trophy-case one, which in a cluster this tight is enough to settle it at sixth.

The Horseshoe sells out one of the most storied programs in college football, but it is mid-pack on raw capacity among the 102,000-seat tier.

Ohio Stadium, universally known as "The Horseshoe," opened on October 7, 1922, making it 103 years old, and has been renovated repeatedly since, most significantly between 1998 and 2001. It seats 102,780 in Columbus and its record crowd hit 110,045, more than 7,000 over its official capacity thanks to standing room, for one of the most successful programs in college football. Its pregame Script Ohio, in which the 200-plus-member marching band spells the word out in cursive and a sousaphone player dots the "i," is among the sport's most recognized rituals.

Near-perfect fill, strong prestige, and easy stadium access lift it above the similarly sized venues around it. It finishes fifth in a cluster so tight that only 459 seats separate it from Kyle Field below and Tiger Stadium, and the composite scores of the middle four are packed within a single point of one another. What edges Ohio Stadium above Kyle Field and Tiger Stadium is a marginally higher prestige and access pairing: the Buckeyes' national profile and Columbus's easy logistics both grade a notch above. In a tier this compressed, those small advantages are decisive, which is exactly what the composite is designed to surface once raw capacity has done its work.

Tiger Stadium's night-game atmosphere is the stuff of legend, but it is the smallest of the top-tier college venues by raw seats.

Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge opened in 1924 and has grown from an original capacity of 12,000 to 102,321 through at least seven major expansions across a century. Known as Death Valley, it is widely regarded as the most intimidating night-game environment in the sport: in 2013 the NCAA ranked it the loudest stadium in all of college football, and the crowd noise from a 1988 touchdown famously registered on the seismograph in LSU's geology building next door. It cost just $1.8 million to build in 1924.

That is why its atmosphere pillar scores 9.5, tied for the loudest here, and its fill rate 9.5 as well: LSU home nights sell out and stay standing. Those marks are enough to edge it past the marginally larger Ohio Stadium, which seats 459 more, into fourth. On raw capacity Tiger Stadium is the smallest of this 102,000-seat tier, trailing Kyle Field by 412 seats, but the composite weights what actually happens inside the walls, and a packed, deafening, seismograph-shaking house is exactly what the fill-rate and atmosphere pillars reward. Death Valley is the clearest case on this list of a stadium punching above its seat count.

Beaver Stadium's White Out is one of the great spectacles in sport, but its more remote location holds its access pillar slightly below the others.

Beaver Stadium in University Park seats 106,572, making it the third-largest here and the second-largest in the United States. It opened in 1960 with a capacity of just 69,000 and has been expanded 12 times since, with lights added in 1984 and a major renovation running from 2024 to 2027. That is a growth of 37,572 seats over its lifetime. Its record crowd of 111,030 exceeded the official capacity by more than 4,000, and it seats 3,792 more than Ohio Stadium three places below it. Its signature White Out games, when the entire crowd wears white, are regularly voted among the best atmospheres in all of sport.

It sells out reliably and the spectacle is genuinely unmatched, so its capacity and fill pillars both score strongly, and its atmosphere pillar of 9.5 ties the loudest venues on the list. What keeps it third rather than higher is access. Beaver Stadium sits in Happy Valley, a relatively remote part of central Pennsylvania roughly three hours from the nearest major city, which nudges its access pillar down a touch below the more centrally located Michigan Stadium 1,029 seats above it. In a top three separated by barely a tenth of a point between second and third, that logistical friction is the entire margin, which is why the composite drops it just behind The Big House despite an atmosphere many rank as the best in the country.

The Big House combines the largest US capacity with near-perfect attendance, but it still trails the world's largest cricket stadium on raw size and global-event prestige.

Michigan Stadium, "The Big House," seats 107,601 in Ann Arbor, the largest stadium in the United States and the largest American football venue in the world. It opened on October 1, 1927 with a capacity of 72,000 and cost $950,000 to build, then grew through expansions in 1928, 1949, 1956, 1973, 1992, 1998 and 2010. Its record crowd of 115,109, set against Notre Dame, is the largest attendance ever recorded at an American football game, and with temporary additions it routinely clears 110,000.

The combination of the biggest US capacity, near-perfect fill, real national prestige, and easy access makes it the strongest all-around venue here after the cricket colossus. Its fill-rate pillar scores 9.5 and its capacity pillar is the highest of any American stadium on the list. It ranks second for one simple reason: exactly one venue on Earth is bigger, the Narendra Modi Stadium, which is 24,399 seats larger and also stages a global championship that Ann Arbor cannot match. Strip out that single cricket giant and Michigan Stadium would top this ranking outright. It is the best all-round stadium in the sport it belongs to, held to second only by a venue playing an entirely different game.

The Narendra Modi Stadium is the largest in the world and hosts cricket's biggest occasions, but it fills mainly for marquee matches rather than a packed weekly calendar, which trims its fill-rate pillar.

The Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad is the largest stadium in the world, seating 132,000, some 18,719 more than the second-largest venue on Earth. It was built between 2015 and 2020 at a cost of ₹800 crore, about 84 million US dollars, on a 63-acre site, replacing an earlier stadium demolished in 2015. Designed by the architecture firm Populous, it hosted the 2023 Cricket World Cup final and the 2026 Men's T20 World Cup final, occasions watched by hundreds of millions, which gives it the highest prestige pillar on this list at 9.5. Its record crowd of 111,989 turned out not for cricket but for a Coldplay concert.

It takes the top spot on the strength of sheer size and the magnitude of the events it stages. The one thing that keeps its score from running away is fill rate, scored at 7.5: it packs out for marquee cricket but does not host the relentless weekly sellouts of an American college stadium, where a program plays six or seven guaranteed home dates every autumn. That is why Michigan Stadium, 24,399 seats smaller, finishes within striking distance rather than being buried. Even so, the world's biggest venue, hosting the world's biggest cricket matches, is a clear number one. It just is not a runaway, and that restraint is the entire point of scoring more than capacity alone.

## The Bottom Line on the Largest Stadiums

Capacity makes the list, but it does not win it outright. The Narendra Modi Stadium takes the top spot on sheer size and the prestige of hosting a Cricket World Cup final, even though it fills only for marquee fixtures. Right behind it sit the American college football giants, smaller on paper but packed to six-figure crowds a dozen Saturdays a year, which is why a 107,000-seat stadium that always sells out outranks a 113,000-seat stadium that almost never does.

That outlier is the real story. Rungrado is the second-largest stadium on Earth and the only one here without a regular sporting tenant to fill it. Built for mass choreographed spectacles rather than ticketed crowds, it is enormous and almost always empty, which drops it from second by size to last by the full picture. Size impresses. A full house is what actually makes a stadium feel like the biggest place on Earth.

The Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad, India, with a capacity of 132,000. It is primarily a cricket venue and hosted the 2023 Cricket World Cup final.

Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in North Korea seats 113,281 but has no regular sporting tenant and is rarely full, so once fill rate and prestige are scored it drops to last on the WorldRankd composite.

Michigan Stadium, "The Big House," in Ann Arbor, seating 107,601. It is the largest American football stadium in the world and sells out routinely.

Six of the eight largest here are US college football stadiums, all seating over 101,000. The two non-American venues are India's Narendra Modi Stadium (cricket) and North Korea's Rungrado.

Biggest Stadium in the World: Top 10 Largest & Capacity - Daily Press UK

Wednesday, 22 July 2026UK news · Politics · Business · Culture · Tech About Us Our Team Sources Contact Newsletter

You ask “which is the biggest stadium in the world” and instantly get half a dozen different answers. The truth depends on whether you measure by seat count, total land area, or sport-specific records — and the top spot shifts depending on who you ask.

Largest stadium in the world (capacity): Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, Pyongyang (114,000) · Largest cricket stadium: Narendra Modi Stadium, Ahmedabad (132,000) · Largest football-only stadium: Camp Nou, Barcelona (99,354) · Largest venue by area: Indianapolis Motor Speedway (559 acres)

## Quick snapshot

1Confirmed facts

- Rungrado 1st of May Stadium – 114,000 official capacity (WorldAtlas geography & sports reference)
- Narendra Modi Stadium – 132,000 (WorldAtlas)
- Camp Nou – 99,354 (Compare the Market consumer research)

2What’s unclear

- Whether Rungrado can actually hold 150,000 with standing room
- Salt Lake Stadium capacity: 120,000 vs 85,000 after 2011 renovation
- Ohio Stadium: figures vary from 102,780 to 104,900

3Timeline signal

- Camp Nou renovation aims for 105,000 by 2026
- No stadium currently reaches 200,000 capacity
- Proposed super‑stadiums in China and Middle East could redraw rankings

4What’s next

- Camp Nou expansion will push Europe’s biggest football stadium past 100,000
- New venues for 2030 World Cup may challenge top-10 lists
- Standing-room vs all-seated definitions could standardize

Seven stadiums, one pattern: the top spot depends entirely on the metric you choose.

| Stadium | Official capacity | Primary use | Location |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rungrado 1st of May Stadium | 114,000 (expandable to 150,000) | Multi‑purpose | Pyongyang, North Korea |
| Narendra Modi Stadium | 132,000 | Cricket | Ahmedabad, India |
| Melbourne Cricket Ground | 100,024 | Multi‑purpose | Melbourne, Australia |
| Camp Nou | 99,354 | Football (soccer) | Barcelona, Spain |
| Salt Lake Stadium | 85,000 (post‑2011) | Multi‑purpose | Kolkata, India |
| Michigan Stadium | 107,601 | American football | Ann Arbor, USA |
| Indianapolis Motor Speedway | ~257,000 (seats + infield) | Motorsport | Speedway, USA |

The implication: capacity numbers are rarely apples-to-apples, and the “biggest” label shifts with context.

## Which is the largest stadium in the world?

### Rungrado 1st of May Stadium overview

- Opened in 1989 on an island in the Taedong River, Pyongyang (Wikipedia open encyclopedia)
- Official capacity: 114,000; expandable to 150,000 with standing room
- Hosts mass games, football matches, and political events

### Capacity and design features

- 10-storey structure with 16 arches forming a petal-like roof
- Standing-room configurations are contentious: some sources claim up to 150,000 (WorldAtlas)
- Comparisons to Narendra Modi Stadium (132,000) and Melbourne Cricket Ground (100,024) (WorldAtlas)

### How it compares to other large stadiums

- Narendra Modi Stadium surpasses it in official seated capacity
- Michigan Stadium (107,601) ranks third globally (WorldAtlas)
- Rungrado remains the largest when counting potential standing-room expansion

What this means: the “world’s largest” label depends on whether you count seats or total bodies.

The paradox

Rungrado claims the top spot if you allow standing room, but Narendra Modi Stadium takes it on strictly seated capacity — a split that fuels endless debate.

## What are the top 10 biggest stadiums in the world?

### Number 1: Rungrado 1st of May Stadium

- 114,000 seated; 150,000 at maximum (WorldAtlas)

### Number 2: Narendra Modi Stadium

- 132,000 seats; largest cricket stadium (WorldAtlas)

### Number 3: Michigan Stadium

- 107,601 seats; home of Michigan Wolverines football (WorldAtlas)

### Number 4: Beaver Stadium

- 106,572 seats; Penn State Nittany Lions (WorldAtlas)

### Number 5: Ohio Stadium

- 102,780–104,900 seats (source-dependent) (WorldAtlas)

### Number 6: Kyle Field

- 102,733 seats; Texas A&M (WorldAtlas)

### Number 7: Tiger Stadium

- 102,321 seats; LSU (WorldAtlas)

### Number 8: Neyland Stadium

- 101,915 seats; University of Tennessee (WorldAtlas)

### Number 9: Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium

- 100,119 seats; University of Texas (WorldAtlas)

### Number 10: Bryant-Denny Stadium

- 100,077 seats (WorldAtlas) or 101,821 (other sources) (WorldAtlas)

The pattern: American college football venues dominate the top 10, but their capacities are tightly packed, with only a few thousand seats separating positions 4 through 10.

## What are the top 20 biggest stadiums in the world?

### The top 20 ranked by capacity

Beyond the top 10, the list includes: Melbourne Cricket Ground (100,024), Camp Nou (99,354), FNB Stadium (94,736), Rose Bowl (92,542), Wembley Stadium (90,000), Estádio do Maracanã (78,838), and others. Full data from Wikipedia’s list of stadiums by capacity community-edited database.

### Notable stadiums outside the top 10

- Azteca Stadium (Mexico City) – 87,523
- Salt Lake Stadium (Kolkata) – 85,000 after renovation (Compare the Market)
- Bukit Jalil National Stadium (Kuala Lumpur) – 87,411

The catch: many of these stadiums are multi‑purpose, and some have variable configurations that change their official capacity for different events.

## What stadium has 200,000 capacity?

### Stadiums with the highest capacities

No modern stadium currently holds 200,000 spectators. The largest capacities top out around 150,000 (Rungrado with standing). The ancient Roman Colosseum held an estimated 50,000–80,000, far short of the 200,000 mark.

### Why 200,000 is not yet achieved

- Safety regulations cap standing densities
- All-seated configurations limit numbers
- Proposed super‑stadiums in China and the Middle East have been discussed but not built

The trade‑off: building a 200,000‑seat venue would require enormous real estate and modern crowd management systems that don’t yet exist at that scale.

The upshot

No existing stadium reaches 200,000, and none are under construction to do so. The “200,000‑seat dream” remains a hypothetical for now.

## Which football stadium has 150,000 capacity?

### The largest football-specific stadiums

- Camp Nou (99,354) is the largest dedicated football stadium (Compare the Market)
- Wembley (90,000) and Twickenham (82,000) are large but smaller

### Multi-purpose stadiums used for football

- Salt Lake Stadium (85,000 after renovation) hosts football but is not a club‑specific venue
- Rungrado hosts football matches but is not a football‑only stadium
- No football‑specific stadium reaches 150,000

Why this matters: fans looking for the biggest true football experience will max out at Camp Nou — and that’s set to grow to 105,000 after renovation.

## What is the biggest stadium in the world by area?

### Stadiums with the largest land area

- Indianapolis Motor Speedway covers 559 acres, making it the largest sports venue by area (Wikipedia)
- Texas Motor Speedway covers 400+ acres
- Autódromo José Carlos Pace (Interlagos) covers over 1,000 acres as a racing circuit

### Difference between capacity and area

Capacity and area are often conflated. The Indianapolis Motor Speedway can hold roughly 257,000 people (including infield), far exceeding any traditional stadium, but its primary purpose is motorsport rather than field sports.

The pattern: area records belong to racetracks, not stadiums. For conventional sports, the Narendra Modi Stadium’s 132,000 seats in a relatively compact footprint is the space-efficient champion.

## Clarity check: confirmed facts vs what’s uncertain

### Confirmed facts

- Rungrado 1st of May Stadium official capacity is 114,000 (WorldAtlas)
- Narendra Modi Stadium is the largest cricket stadium at 132,000 (WorldAtlas)
- Camp Nou is the largest football‑only stadium in Europe at 99,354 (Compare the Market)
- Indianapolis Motor Speedway is the largest sports venue by area at 559 acres (Wikipedia)

### What’s uncertain

- Whether Rungrado can actually hold 150,000 with standing (WorldAtlas)
- Salt Lake Stadium’s true post‑renovation capacity (85,000 vs 120,000) (Compare the Market)
- Ohio Stadium and Bryant-Denny Stadium show differing numbers across sources (WorldAtlas)
- Future stadium projects in China and Middle East may change rankings

“The Rungrado 1st of May Stadium is the largest stadium in the world by capacity, though its exact configuration is often debated.”

— StadiumDB.com specialist venue database

“Camp Nou’s renovation will push its capacity to 105,000, reclaiming the top spot among football‑specific stadiums.”

— Compare the Market consumer research

“Narendra Modi Stadium’s 132,000 seats make it the undisputed largest cricket venue globally.”

— WorldAtlas geography & sports reference

“The top 10 list is dominated by American college football stadiums, but capacity gaps are narrow.”

— Wikipedia’s list of stadiums by capacity community-edited database

The “biggest stadium” title means different things depending on whether you count seats, bodies, land, or sport. For fans in Europe planning a bucket‑list visit, the clearest answer is Camp Nou before its renovation — but capacity alone doesn’t tell the whole story. The choice is simple: pick your metric, then pick your stadium.

Additional sources

For readers interested in broader rankings, this article provides a detailed breakdown of the worlds largest stadiums by capacity, including Rungrado and Narendra Modi Stadium.

## Frequently asked questions

How is stadium capacity measured?

Capacity is usually the number of fixed seats, but some stadiums include standing areas, temporary seating, or “maximum occupancy” for special events.

Does standing room count toward capacity?

In many official lists, capacity includes only seated spaces. Standing room is often quoted separately, creating discrepancies.

Which stadium has the most seats (all-seated)?

Narendra Modi Stadium with 132,000 seats is the largest all-seated venue.

When was Rungrado 1st of May Stadium built?

It opened in 1989.

What is the capacity of the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta?

It holds 71,000 for most events, expandable to 75,000 for major games.

Is the Azteca Stadium one of the top 10 largest?

Azteca Stadium (Mexico City) has 87,523 seats, placing it outside the top 10 but within the top 20.

What is the biggest stadium in South America?

Estádio do Maracanã (Rio de Janeiro) is the largest in South America at 78,838 seats.

Are there any stadiums planned with 200,000 capacity?

No confirmed plans exist. Proposed mega‑projects in China and the Middle East remain speculative.
